The present work’s thermal oxidation of TC21 alloy was performed at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 5, 20, and 50 h durations. Hot corrosion methods in NaCl and NaCl + Na2SO4 salt media were applied to raw (unoxidized) and oxidized samples at 600 and 800 °C for 50 h. Hot corrosion was conducted at 600 °C for 5 cycles with 10-h steps. The best oxide layer thickness was observed at 800 °C, which increased with increased oxidation time and temperature. The surface hardness of the oxide layer at 800 °C was 900 ± 60 HV0.05 owing to the formation of TiO2 and Al2O3 phases. Raw material hardness was 342 ± 20 HV0.05, increasing threefold due to thermal oxidation. In the case of NaCl, weight loss dominated all samples except at 800 °C for 5 h. In the case of NaCl + Na2SO4, weight gain occurred at 600 and 800 °C for 5 h. Weight loss occurred for the raw samples and those processed at 800 °C for 20 and 50 h, where the oxide layer flaked off. Surface hardness increased upon hot corrosion testing because of the formation of brittle phases, such as TiO2 and Na4Ti5O12. Samples that oxidized at 800 °C for 5 h had the highest hardness and corrosion resistance. These alloys have good properties such as strength, toughness, fatigue, corrosion, and thermal stability. However, a major factor affecting mechanical properties is microstructure. The important phases of titanium alloys are α-phase, hexagonal close-packed structure (HCP), and β-phase, body-centered cubic (BCC). α-β alloys are the most extensively used titanium alloys. Many microstructures of titanium alloys are formed, such as lamellar, equiaxed, and bimodal. The microstructure can be changed using different heat treatment regimes and cooling media. The microstructural parameters include morphology, grain size, volume fraction, and phase distribution13,14. Generally, the equiaxed microstructure provides good strength, high ductility, and high fatigue resistance15–17. Mechanical characteristics are the most important performance factor for titanium applications such as movable and fixed blades in gas turbines. Biocompatibility is the most crucial element in medicine, such as dental implants and bone scaffolds. Corrosion is the most important property in the petroleum sector, such as fluid transmission tubes. So, the most crucial requirement in the industrial sector is corrosion resistance. In contrast to Ti4+-containing titanium dioxide (TiO2), which has a wide bandgap (∼3.0 eV) and has been widely explored for catalysis and energy applications, titanium sesquioxide (Ti2O3) with an intermediate valence state (Ti3+) possesses an ultranarrow bandgap (∼0.1 eV) and has been much less investigated. Although the importance of Ti3+ to the applications of TiO2 is widely recognized, the connection between TiO2 and Ti2O3 and the transformation pathway remain unknown. Herein, we investigate the oxidation-induced structural, phase, and property evolution of Ti2O3 using a complementary suite of microscopic and spectroscopic tools. Interestingly, transformation pathways to both rutile and anatase TiO2 are identified, which sensitively depend on oxidation conditions. Unique Ti2O3/TiO2 core–shell structures with annealing-controlled surface nanostructure formation are observed for the first time. The compositional and structural evolution of Ti2O3/TiO2 particles is accompanied by continuously tuned optical and electrical properties. While it is observed that the grey contrast coloured α grains are coaxial in the microstructures, it is seen that there are black contrast coloured β grains at the grain boundaries. However, in oxidised Titanium Grade 5, it is possible to observe that the α structure becomes larger, and the number and density of the structure increases. Small-sized structures can be seen inside the growing α particles and on the β particles. These structures are predicted to be Al-Ti/Al-V secondary phases. The nonoxidised alloy matrix and the OL layer exhibited a macrolevel hardness of 335 ± 3.21 HB and 353 ± 1.62 HB, respectively. The heat treatment increased Vickers microhardness by 13% in polished and etched nonoxidised and oxidised alloys, from 309 ± 2.08 HV1 to 352 ± 1.43 HV1. The Vickers microhardness value of the oxidised sample was 528 ± 1.74 HV1, as a 50% increase was noted. According to their tensile properties, oxidised alloys showed a better result compared to nonoxidised alloys. While the peak stress in the oxidised alloy was 1028.40 MPa, in the nonoxidised alloy, this value was 1027.20 MPa. It is seen that the peak stresses of both materials are close to each other, and the result of the oxidised alloy is slightly better. When we look at the breaking strain to characterise the deformation behaviour in the materials, it is 0.084 mm/mm in the oxidised alloy; In the nonoxidised alloy, it is 0.066 mm/mm. When we look at the stress at offset yield of the two alloys, it is 694.56 MPa in the oxidised alloy; it was found to be 674.092 MPa in the nonoxidised alloy. According to their compressive test properties, the maximum compressive strength is 2164.32 MPa in the oxidised alloy; in the nonoxidised alloy, it is 1531.52 MPa. While the yield strength is 972.50 MPa in oxidised Titanium Grade 5, it was found to be 934.16 MPa in nonoxidised Titanium Grade 5. When the compressive deformation oxidised alloy is 100.01%, in the nonoxidised alloy, it is 68.50%. This material’s weight loss and wear coefficient at the end of 10,000 m are 0.127 ± 0.0002 g and (63.45 ± 0.15) × 10−8 g/Nm, respectively. The highest weight loss and worst wear resistance have been observed in the nonoxidised alloy. The weight loss and wear coefficients at the end of 10,000 m are 0.140 ± 0.0003 g and (69.75 ± 0.09) × 10−8 g/Nm, respectively. The commercial applicability of the Kroll method caused the US armed forces to become interested in titanium in 1947. This alloy was initially manufactured in 1952 for use in the engine combustion chamber and the engine connection point on the wings of DC-7-type aircraft [1]. Titanium also has a higher melting point than iron, at 1668 °C. Furthermore, titanium and its alloys are highly prized engineering materials nowadays for their exceptional corrosion resistance and strength-to-density ratios [2]. Submission received: 27 May 2019 / Revised: 1 August 2019 / Accepted: 2 August 2019 / Published: 5 August 2019 Abstract The need for metallic biomaterials will always remain high with their growing demand in joint replacement in the aging population. This creates need for the market and researchers to focus on the development and advancement of the biometals. Desirable characteristics such as excellent biocompatibility, high strength, comparable elastic modulus with bones, good corrosion resistance, and high wear resistance are the significant issues to address for medical implants, particularly load-bearing orthopedic implants. The widespread use of titanium alloys in biomedical implants create a big demand to identify and assess the behavior and performance of these alloys when used in the human body. Being the most commonly used metal alloy in the fabrication of medical implants, mainly because of its good biocompatibility and corrosion resistance together with its high strength to weight ratio, the tribological behavior of these alloys have always been an important subject for study. Titanium alloys with improved wear resistance will of course enhance the longevity of implants in the body. In this paper, tribological performance of titanium alloys (medical grades) is reviewed. Various methods of surface modifications employed for titanium alloys are also discussed in the context of wear behavior. 1. Introduction The growth of aging population has caused an increasing demand for using metallic biomaterials in the manufacturing process of medical implants (e.g., hip [1,2] and knee [2,3] implants). Metals (and metal alloys) including stainless steels, Co-Cr-Mo, and titanium alloys are most commonly used in load-bearing implants because of their favorable features such as high strength, stiffness, and toughness. Specifically, titanium alloys are more commonly used owing to their better biocompatibility and mechanical strength characteristics [4]. For instance, the lower wear rate was reported as a reason for the popularity of Ti-6Al-4V alloy although its high Young’s modulus may lead to stress shielding, incompatibility with the host bone, and bone resorption [5,6,7]. Increasing the risk of loosening at the implant-bone interference contributes to the growth of revision surgeries [8]. Presence of vanadium as a toxic threat for human tissues influences the activity of inflammatory response cells. In addition, the risk of developing Alzheimer’s disease may enhance with aluminum [9,10,11]. Replacing vanadium (V) by non-toxic elements such as niobium (Nb) and iron (Fe) in Ti-6Al-4Fe and Ti-6Al-4Nb resulted in improved corrosion resistance [12]. Some features of newly developed β-type titanium alloys have been reported in several studies including better mechanical strength, greater biocompatibility, low stiffness, and non-allergic characteristic in comparison with conventional Ti alloys [13]. However, low wear resistance and high friction coefficients were noted as the major issues of these alloys in implants’ design and manufacture [14,15,16]. To overcome these shortcomings some surface engineering techniques have been performed, such as nano-grained surface, laser surface texturing, coatings, and oxidation, as solutions [17]. This paper aims to review the literature on the tribological behavior of Ti alloys including new generation ones, and the effect of surface modification methods on the friction and wear resistance of these alloys. 2. Wear Behavior of Ti Alloys (Without Surface Modifications) Generally, a poor tribological performance with low surface hardness has been reported for titanium alloys that are used in biomedical implants [18,19,20]. High coefficients of friction (COF), intense adhesive wear, and low abrasion resistance are regarded as the adverse effects of their tribological behavior [21]. Mechanical sliding between titanium alloys (or a titanium alloy and another material) may lead to wear damage over the surface by disrupting the protective oxide layer, mainly in the presence of a third body at the interface [22]. High reactivity of titanium alloys causes a rapid change of the oxide surface layer to oxidative environment; consequently, it may lead to a removal during the sliding of the two contacting surfaces [22]. After investigation of wear behavior by ball-on-disc and pin-on-disc tribometers, it was reported that the volume loss of titanium alloys increases with rising sliding speed. This study listed Ti-6Al-7Nb and Ti-6Al-4V in a decreasing order based on their estimated wear values at any specific sliding speed [22]. The results of a study performed by De Viteri and Fuentes [23] showed that the protective oxide layer can be removed from the surface of metals. This phenomenon occurs by applying contact loads which allows metals to have interaction with the surrounding environment (or the adjacent material). Thermal oxidation of Ti64 (Ti6Al4V) changes its surface structure and oxide layer in a way that is strongly dependent on temperature, time, and oxidation conditions. The most consistent picture from the evidence is that oxidation forms a protective oxide layer on the surface, but this layer can vary in morphology, thickness, porosity, and phase composition depending on the process parameters.

On the surface features side, oxidation can produce oxide layers that are initially dense, but under prolonged exposure or higher temperatures, they can become porous, cracked, and even rougher. The evidence indicates that isothermal oxidation after 300 h produces a dense oxide layer that contributes to increased resistance to further oxidization [N1-R2]. However, oxide layer de-bonding and oxide-related damage are also noted at excessively high temperatures, which can lead to loss of adhesion or damage to the oxide layer [N6-R1]. Additional evidence suggests that oxide layer thickness and grain size improve with increasing temperature, but the same temperature can also trigger cracking or porosity in the oxide layer [N6-R2]. The literature also notes that oxide layers formed by thermal oxidation can be thick, porous, cracked, and rough, especially under high-temperature conditions [N1-R4]. Taken together, the surface features formed during oxidation are not uniform: oxide, pores, cracks, and roughness can all appear, with the relative dominance of each feature depending on temperature and time.

Oxidation depth, thickness, porosity, and roughness clearly vary with temperature and time. The evidence shows that oxide layer thickness increases with both oxidation time and temperature. For example, in TC21 alloy oxidation at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 5, 20, and 50 h, the best oxide layer thickness was observed at 800 °C, and it increased with longer oxidation time and higher temperature [N1-F1]. Likewise, oxidation at 800 °C for 5 h produced a 900 ± 60 HV0.05 surface hardness due to the formation of TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ phases [N1-F1]. The same source also reports that weight loss in Ti64 decreases with increasing oxidation temperature, which is consistent with a denser and more protective oxide forming as temperature rises [N3-R3]. On the other hand, higher temperature can also reduce the protective quality of the oxide layer: in some contexts, TiO₂ is described as not fully protective and can spall off [N1-F1]. Porosity and roughness are also temperature-dependent: the evidence suggests that higher temperature can increase oxide grain size and improve uniformity of coverage, but it can also lead to cracking and oxide de-bonding [N6-R2], while lower-temperature and shorter-time oxidation may produce oxide layers that are not thick enough for some tribological applications [N6-R5]. Overall, the oxide layer becomes thicker and more uniform with higher temperature, but the surface can become rougher and more porous as oxidation progresses.

The oxide phases formed and how they evolve with heating are also important. The evidence indicates that TiO₂ is the primary oxide formed on titanium alloys, and it is described as the stable, adhesive, and protective layer formed by inward oxygen diffusion [N1-F1]. However, oxidation-induced phase evolution is more complex than a simple TiO₂ layer: a separate source notes that titanium can form multiple oxides, including TiO₂, Ti₃O₅, TiO, and Ti₂O₃, and that all these oxides have very different properties [N2-R5]. Another source specifically describes oxidation-induced structural, phase, and property evolution, noting that TiO₂ polymorphs coexist up to 800 °C, and the complete conversion to the rutile phase occurs at higher temperatures [N2-F2]. This means that during thermal oxidation, the oxide layer is not static; it can transition between different polymorphs and can contain a mixture of oxides depending on the oxidation conditions. The evidence also shows that TiO₂ is not always fully protective; in some contexts, it can be brittle and prone to spallation, while Al₂O₃ is noted as affecting hot corrosion resistance [N1-F1]. Therefore, oxidation does not simply produce one oxide phase; it generates a phase sequence that evolves with temperature and time, with TiO₂ being the dominant protective oxide, but other oxides and polymorphs also playing a role in the oxide layer composition.

In summary, thermal oxidation of Ti64 changes the surface structure by forming an oxide layer that can be dense, porous, cracked, and rough, with these features becoming more pronounced at higher temperatures and longer oxidation times. Oxide thickness increases with temperature and time, while porosity, roughness, and cracking can also increase. The oxide layer is primarily TiO₂, but the oxidation process also produces other titanium oxides and polymorphs that evolve with heating. The overall effect is that the surface morphology and oxide composition are not fixed; they are strongly shaped by the oxidation environment [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R5][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5][N1-F1].

Thermal oxidation of Ti64 generally increases hardness, but the evidence also shows that the relationship between oxide layer thickness, phase composition, and mechanical response is nuanced and temperature-dependent.

The most direct evidence for hardness change is that oxidation increases hardness. Thermal oxidation of Ti64 (Ti6Al4V) changes its surface structure and oxide layer in a way that is strongly dependent on temperature, time, and oxidation conditions. The most consistent picture from the evidence is that oxidation forms a protective oxide layer on the surface, but this layer can vary in morphology, thickness, porosity, and phase composition depending on the process parameters.

On the surface features side, oxidation can produce oxide layers that are initially dense, but under prolonged exposure or higher temperatures, they can become porous, cracked, and even rougher. The evidence indicates that isothermal oxidation after 300 h produces a dense oxide layer that contributes to increased resistance to further oxidization [N1-R2]. However, oxide layer de-bonding and oxide-related damage are also noted at excessively high temperatures, which can lead to loss of adhesion or damage to the oxide layer [N6-R1]. Additional evidence suggests that oxide layer thickness and grain size improve with increasing temperature, but the same temperature can also trigger cracking or porosity in the oxide layer [N6-R2]. The literature also notes that oxide layers formed by thermal oxidation can be thick, porous, cracked, and rough, especially under high-temperature conditions [N1-R4]. Taken together, the surface features formed during oxidation are not uniform: oxide, pores, cracks, and roughness can all appear, with the relative dominance of each feature depending on temperature and time.

Oxidation depth, thickness, porosity, and roughness clearly vary with temperature and time. The evidence shows that oxide layer thickness increases with both oxidation time and temperature. For example, in TC21 alloy oxidation at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 5, 20, and 50 h, the best oxide layer thickness was observed at 800 °C, and it increased with longer oxidation time and higher temperature [N1-F1]. Likewise, oxidation at 800 °C for 5 h produced a 900 ± 60 HV0.05 surface hardness due to the formation of TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ phases [N1-F1]. The same source also reports that weight loss in Ti64 decreases with increasing oxidation temperature, which is consistent with a denser and more protective oxide forming as temperature rises [N3-R3]. On the other hand, higher temperature can also reduce the protective quality of the oxide layer: in some contexts, TiO₂ is described as not fully protective and can spall off [N1-F1]. Porosity and roughness are also temperature-dependent: the evidence suggests that higher temperature can increase oxide grain size and improve uniformity of coverage, but it can also lead to cracking and oxide de-bonding [N6-R2], while lower-temperature and shorter-time oxidation may produce oxide layers that are not thick enough for some tribological applications [N6-R5]. Overall, the oxide layer becomes thicker and more uniform with higher temperature, but the surface can become rougher and more porous as oxidation progresses.

The oxide phases formed and how they evolve with heating are also important. The evidence indicates that TiO₂ is the primary oxide formed on titanium alloys, and it is described as the stable, adhesive, and protective layer formed by inward oxygen diffusion [N1-F1]. However, oxidation-induced phase evolution is more complex than a simple TiO₂ layer: a separate source notes that titanium can form multiple oxides, including TiO₂, Ti₃O₅, TiO, and Ti₂O₃, and that all these oxides have very different properties [N2-R5]. Another source specifically describes oxidation-induced structural, phase, and property evolution, noting that TiO₂ polymorphs coexist up to 800 °C, and the complete conversion to the rutile phase occurs at higher temperatures [N2-F2]. This means that during thermal oxidation, the oxide layer is not static; it can transition between different polymorphs and can contain a mixture of oxides depending on the oxidation conditions. The evidence also shows that TiO₂ is not always fully protective; in some contexts, it can be brittle and prone to spallation, while Al₂O₃ is noted as affecting hot corrosion resistance [N1-F1]. Therefore, oxidation does not simply produce one oxide phase; it generates a phase sequence that evolves with temperature and time, with TiO₂ being the dominant protective oxide, but other oxides and polymorphs also playing a role in the oxide layer composition.

In summary, thermal oxidation of Ti64 changes the surface structure by forming an oxide layer that can be dense, porous, cracked, and rough, with these features becoming more pronounced at higher temperatures and longer oxidation times. Oxide thickness increases with temperature and time, while porosity, roughness, and cracking can also increase. The oxide layer is primarily TiO₂, but the oxidation process also produces other titanium oxides and polymorphs that evolve with heating. The overall effect is that the surface morphology and oxide composition are not fixed; they are strongly shaped by the oxidation environment [N1-R1][N1-R2][N1-R4][N2-R5][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5][N1-F1].

Thermal oxidation of Ti64 generally increases hardness, but the evidence also shows that the relationship between oxide layer thickness, phase composition, and mechanical response is nuanced and temperature-dependent.

The most direct evidence for hardness change is that oxidation increases hardness. In the TC21 alloy study, the surface hardness of the oxide layer at 800 °C was 900 ± 60 HV0.05, and the raw material hardness was 342 ± 20 HV0.05, resulting in a threefold increase due to thermal oxidation [N1-F1]. Another source reports that the oxidation process has been shown to improve the tribological properties of Titanium Grade 5 alloy, including a 50% increase in Vickers microhardness for the oxidized sample [N3-F3]. A separate review also states that oxidation of Ti6Al4V leads to significantly increased hardness and wear resistance, with oxidation enhancing hardness during oxidation [N5-R5]. These sources together support the conclusion that oxidation usually increases hardness, not decreases it.

The evidence also indicates that oxide layer thickness and phase composition are important factors in the hardness change. The TC21 study reports that the best oxide layer thickness was observed at 800 °C, and that this temperature and longer oxidation time produced the highest surface hardness [N1-F1]. This suggests a direct relationship between oxide thickness and hardness: thicker oxide layers are associated with higher hardness. In addition, the phase composition matters because the same study notes that TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ phases formed at 800 °C contributed to the hardness increase [N1-F1]. Another source notes that the mechanical properties of oxide layers change with oxidation temperature, and oxide layers are described as effective corrosion barriers and mechanical improvements [N7-R1]. A separate source also states that interstitial diffusion of oxygen in titanium alloys significantly increases hardness at elevated oxidation temperatures [N5-R3]. Together, these findings indicate that both the physical thickness of the oxide layer and its chemical composition—especially the presence of TiO₂ and other protective oxides—contribute to the observed increase in hardness.

Temperature-dependent hardness trends are also present in the literature. The TC21 study shows that the best oxide layer thickness and highest surface hardness occurred at 800 °C, with increasing temperature and oxidation time associated with higher hardness [N1-F1]. The same source also reports that weight loss in Ti64 decreased with increasing oxidation temperature, which is consistent with a more protective and harder oxide layer forming at higher temperatures [N3-R3]. Another source reports that Ti at 750 °C showed the best results, obtaining a hardness value of up to 11.35 GPa, which is 5 times higher than titanium without oxidation [N7-R2]. This suggests that the hardness gain is not simply a one-time effect at a single temperature, but that it varies with temperature. However, the literature is not entirely uniform: one source notes that TO of the Ti-6Al-4V ELI alloy led to an increase in hardness and deformation resistance, but it also mentions that following oxidation, there was a decrease in some mechanical properties, though the exact wording is less explicit about hardness [N7-R4]. Still, the overall trend in the evidence is that higher temperatures and longer oxidation times tend to produce thicker, harder oxide layers, while extreme temperatures can introduce brittleness or spallation that may weaken the oxide layer [N1-F1][N6-R1]. 

In conclusion, oxidation generally increases hardness in Ti64, with oxide layer thickness and phase composition playing a key role in the mechanical response. The evidence also shows that the hardness change is temperature-dependent: higher temperatures often increase hardness, but the relationship is not linear, and extreme conditions can reduce protective quality or introduce brittleness [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R5][N5-R3][N7-R1][N7-R2][N7-R4].

Thermal oxidation of Ti64 generally improves wear resistance, but the evidence also indicates that the tribological performance is strongly influenced by oxide layer structure, contact conditions, and the specific wear mechanism.

The most direct evidence is that oxidation improves wear resistance. One source reports that the oxidation process has been shown to improve the tribological properties of Titanium Grade 5 alloy [N3-R1]. Another source states that oxidation of Ti6Al4V leads to significantly increased hardness and wear resistance [N5-R5], while a separate review explicitly states that the wear resistance of Ti6Al4V is greatly improved due to its complete film layer, shallow furrow, and no tear marks [N5-R1]. A tribology analysis of Ti6Al4V also shows a significant enhancement in wear resistance, with the wear rate of pristine Ti6Al4V reduced by two orders of magnitude [N5-R4]. In addition, a study on Ti-6Al-4V notes that TO-treated material showed a significant improvement in wear resistance in sliding–rolling contact with a steel surface under boundary lubrication [N4-R1]. These findings indicate that oxidation is associated with better wear performance in many contexts.

The evidence also shows that oxide layer structure influences friction and wear mechanisms. The same review notes that high coefficients of friction (COF), intense adhesive wear, and low abrasion resistance are regarded as the adverse effects of titanium alloys’ tribological behavior [N4-F4]. By contrast, oxidation improves the protective oxide layer, which can reduce abrasive wear and mitigate direct metal-to-metal contact. The TC21 study reports that the oxidized sample had the least weight loss after 10,000 m and the best wear resistance, while the nonoxidized alloy had the highest weight loss and worst wear resistance [N3-F3]. Another source explains that the protective oxide layer can be removed during sliding, which can lead to high friction and corrosion [N4-F4], suggesting that the oxide layer acts as a barrier that prevents direct interaction between the surfaces and thereby reduces wear. The evidence also notes that oxide layer formation enhances tribological performance because the oxide is protective and can improve wear resistance [N7-R1].

The literature also indicates that oxidation can alter wear resistance in different contact conditions. In boundary lubrication, the TO-treated material showed significant improvement in wear resistance in sliding–rolling contact with a steel surface [N4-R1]. In dry sliding, titanium alloys are described as having a dramatic rise in wear rate when subjected to stress [N4-F4], and one source reports that the oxidation process improved tribological properties of Titanium Grade 5 alloy [N3-R1]. For fretting wear, the evidence is more indirect but still relevant: one study involves understanding the fretting wear behavior of Ti-6Al-4V alloy under fretting conditions [N8-R2], and another reports that surface texturing and solid lubricants can substantially reduce friction and wear under dry conditions [N8-R3]. While the evidence provided here does not give a direct comparison of oxidation effects across all contact modes, it does show that oxidation tends to be beneficial in boundary lubrication and that the protective oxide layer can reduce wear in dry sliding and fretting-like conditions [N4-R1][N4-F4][N3-R1][N8-R2].

A key difference between conditions is that oxidation can help more in boundary lubrication and wear regimes where direct contact and friction are reduced by the oxide layer, while dry sliding and fretting may still be affected by oxide spallation, oxide removal, or direct metal-to-metal interaction [N4-F4][N4-R1][N8-R2]. Taken together, the surface features formed during oxidation are not uniform: oxide, pores, cracks, and roughness can all appear, with the relative dominance of each feature depending on temperature and time.

Oxidation depth, thickness, porosity, and roughness clearly vary with temperature and time. The evidence shows that oxide layer thickness increases with both oxidation time and temperature. For example, in TC21 alloy oxidation at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 5, 20, and 50 h, the best oxide layer thickness was observed at 800 °C, and it increased with longer oxidation time and higher temperature [N1-F1]. Porosity and roughness are also temperature-dependent: the evidence suggests that higher temperature can increase oxide grain size and improve uniformity of coverage, but it can also lead to cracking and oxide de-bonding [N6-R2], while lower-temperature and shorter-time oxidation may produce oxide layers that are not thick enough for some tribological applications [N6-R5]. The most consistent picture from the evidence is that oxidation forms a protective oxide layer on the surface, but this layer can vary in morphology, thickness, porosity, and phase composition depending on the process parameters.

On the surface features side, oxidation can produce oxide layers that are initially dense, but under prolonged exposure or higher temperatures, they can become porous, cracked, and even rougher. The evidence indicates that isothermal oxidation after 300 h produces a dense oxide layer that contributes to increased resistance to further oxidization [N1-R2]. However, oxide layer de-bonding and oxide-related damage are also noted at excessively high temperatures, which can lead to loss of adhesion or damage to the oxide layer [N6-R1]. Additional evidence suggests that oxide layer thickness and grain size improve with increasing temperature, but the same temperature can also trigger cracking or porosity in the oxide layer [N6-R2]. The literature also notes that oxide layers formed by thermal oxidation can be thick, porous, cracked, and rough, especially under high-temperature conditions [N1-R4]. Taken together, the surface features formed during oxidation are not uniform: oxide, pores, cracks, and roughness can all appear, with the relative dominance of each feature depending on temperature and time.

Oxidation depth, thickness, porosity, and roughness clearly vary with temperature and time. The evidence shows that oxide layer thickness increases with both oxidation time and temperature. For example, in TC21 alloy oxidation at 600, 700, and 800 °C for 5, 20, and 50 h, the best oxide layer thickness was observed at 800 °C, and it increased with longer oxidation time and higher temperature [N1-F1]. Likewise, oxidation at 800 °C for 5 h produced a 900 ± 60 HV0.05 surface hardness due to the formation of TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ phases [N1-F1]. The same source also reports that weight loss in Ti64 decreases with increasing oxidation temperature, which is consistent with a denser and more protective oxide forming as temperature rises [N3-R3]. On the other hand, higher temperature can also reduce the protective quality of the oxide layer: in some contexts, TiO₂ is described as not fully protective and can spall off [N1-F1]. Porosity and roughness are also temperature-dependent: the evidence suggests that higher temperature can increase oxide grain size and improve uniformity of coverage, but it can also lead to cracking and oxide de-bonding [N6-R2], while lower-temperature and shorter-time oxidation may produce oxide layers that are not thick enough for some tribological applications [N6-R5]. Overall, the oxide layer becomes thicker and more uniform with higher temperature, but the surface can become rougher and more porous as oxidation progresses.

The oxide phases formed and how they evolve with heating are also important. The evidence indicates that TiO₂ is the primary oxide formed on titanium alloys, and it is described as the stable, adhesive, and protective layer formed by inward oxygen diffusion [N1-F1]. In summary, thermal oxidation of Ti64 changes the surface structure by forming an oxide layer that can be dense, porous, cracked, and rough, with these features becoming more pronounced at higher temperatures and longer oxidation times. Oxide thickness increases with temperature and time, while porosity, roughness, and cracking can also increase. These sources together support the conclusion that oxidation usually increases hardness, not decreases it.

The evidence also indicates that oxide layer thickness and phase composition are important factors in the hardness change. The TC21 study reports that the best oxide layer thickness was observed at 800 °C, and that this temperature and longer oxidation time produced the highest surface hardness [N1-F1]. This suggests a direct relationship between oxide thickness and hardness: thicker oxide layers are associated with higher hardness. In addition, the phase composition matters because the same study notes that TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ phases formed at 800 °C contributed to the hardness increase [N1-F1]. Another source notes that the mechanical properties of oxide layers change with oxidation temperature, and oxide layers are described as effective corrosion barriers and mechanical improvements [N7-R1]. A separate source also states that interstitial diffusion of oxygen in titanium alloys significantly increases hardness at elevated oxidation temperatures [N5-R3]. Together, these findings indicate that both the physical thickness of the oxide layer and its chemical composition—especially the presence of TiO₂ and other protective oxides—contribute to the observed increase in hardness.

Temperature-dependent hardness trends are also present in the literature. In conclusion, oxidation generally increases hardness in Ti64, with oxide layer thickness and phase composition playing a key role in the mechanical response. The most direct evidence is that oxidation improves wear resistance. One source reports that the oxidation process has been shown to improve the tribological properties of Titanium Grade 5 alloy [N3-R1]. Another source states that oxidation of Ti6Al4V leads to significantly increased hardness and wear resistance [N5-R5], while a separate review explicitly states that the wear resistance of Ti6Al4V is greatly improved due to its complete film layer, shallow furrow, and no tear marks [N5-R1]. A tribology analysis of Ti6Al4V also shows a significant enhancement in wear resistance, with the wear rate of pristine Ti6Al4V reduced by two orders of magnitude [N5-R4]. In addition, a study on Ti-6Al-4V notes that TO-treated material showed a significant improvement in wear resistance in sliding–rolling contact with a steel surface under boundary lubrication [N4-R1]. These findings indicate that oxidation is associated with better wear performance in many contexts.

The evidence also shows that oxide layer structure influences friction and wear mechanisms. The same review notes that high coefficients of friction (COF), intense adhesive wear, and low abrasion resistance are regarded as the adverse effects of titanium alloys’ tribological behavior [N4-F4]. By contrast, oxidation improves the protective oxide layer, which can reduce abrasive wear and mitigate direct metal-to-metal contact. The TC21 study reports that the oxidized sample had the least weight loss after 10,000 m and the best wear resistance, while the nonoxidized alloy had the highest weight loss and worst wear resistance [N3-F3]. Another source explains that the protective oxide layer can be removed during sliding, which can lead to high friction and corrosion [N4-F4], suggesting that the oxide layer acts as a barrier that prevents direct interaction between the surfaces and thereby reduces wear. The evidence also notes that oxide layer formation enhances tribological performance because the oxide is protective and can improve wear resistance [N7-R1].

The literature also indicates that oxidation can alter wear resistance in different contact conditions. In boundary lubrication, the TO-treated material showed significant improvement in wear resistance in sliding–rolling contact with a steel surface [N4-R1]. In dry sliding, titanium alloys are described as having a dramatic rise in wear rate when subjected to stress [N4-F4], and one source reports that the oxidation process improved tribological properties of Titanium Grade 5 alloy [N3-R1]. For fretting wear, the evidence is more indirect but still relevant: one study involves understanding the fretting wear behavior of Ti-6Al-4V alloy under fretting conditions [N8-R2], and another reports that surface texturing and solid lubricants can substantially reduce friction and wear under dry conditions [N8-R3]. While the evidence provided here does not give a direct comparison of oxidation effects across all contact modes, it does show that oxidation tends to be beneficial in boundary lubrication and that the protective oxide layer can reduce wear in dry sliding and fretting-like conditions [N4-R1][N4-F4][N3-R1][N8-R2].

A key difference between conditions is that oxidation can help more in boundary lubrication and wear regimes where direct contact and friction are reduced by the oxide layer, while dry sliding and fretting may still be affected by oxide spallation, oxide removal, or direct metal-to-metal interaction [N4-F4][N4-R1][N8-R2]. The evidence also suggests that the oxide layer is not always perfectly protective; in some contexts, it can be brittle or prone to spallation, which may reduce its effectiveness [N1-F1]. Overall, oxidation generally improves wear resistance, but the extent of improvement depends on oxide layer quality, contact conditions, and whether the oxide remains intact during sliding.

In conclusion, oxidation usually improves wear resistance in Ti64, especially in boundary lubrication and sliding conditions, because the oxide layer reduces direct contact and mitigates abrasive wear [N3-R1][N5-R1][N5-R4][N4-R1][N4-F4]. Oxide layer structure matters because a protective oxide can reduce friction and wear, while spallation or removal can reduce effectiveness [N4-F4][N1-F1]. The evidence also suggests that oxidation can be beneficial in dry sliding and fretting, but the specific wear mechanism and contact conditions can alter the magnitude of improvement [N4-R1][N4-F4][N8-R2].

The evidence shows that oxidation forms an oxide layer, but the quality and performance of that layer depend on the oxide phases present, the surface morphology developed, and the oxidation conditions such as temperature and time.

Oxidation-induced phase changes and surface morphology jointly affect hardness and wear resistance through a complex interplay of protective and damaging effects. On the surface structure side, oxidation can produce dense, porous, cracked, and rough oxide layers, with higher temperatures and longer times usually leading to thicker oxide layers but also more porosity and roughness [N1-R2][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The same evidence indicates that oxide layer thickness increases with both temperature and time, while porosity and roughness can also increase, especially at excessively high temperatures [N1-F1][N6-R1]. This means that the oxide layer can be both beneficial and problematic: it can protect and harden the surface, but it can also become brittle, spall off, or degrade the surface quality [N1-F1][N6-R1].

On the phase composition side, oxidation produces not just a single oxide, but a mixture of titanium oxides that evolves with heating. The evidence notes that titanium can form multiple oxides including TiO₂, TiO, Ti₃O₅, and Ti₂O₃, and that these oxides have very different properties [N2-R5]. Another source shows that TiO₂ polymorphs coexist up to 800 °C, and complete conversion to rutile occurs at higher temperatures [N2-F2]. The TC21 study also explicitly states that TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ phases formed at 800 °C contributed to the hardness increase [N1-F1]. This means that the oxide layer is not static; it changes with temperature, and the presence of TiO₂ and other oxides can influence the mechanical response. TiO₂ is described as the stable, adhesive, and protective layer formed by inward oxygen diffusion [N1-F1], but it can also be brittle and prone to spallation [N1-F1]. Al₂O₃ is noted as affecting hot corrosion resistance [N1-F1], suggesting that phase composition matters for both mechanical and environmental performance.

Taken together, these phase changes and surface morphology changes jointly affect hardness and wear resistance. Oxidation generally increases hardness, with evidence showing a threefold increase in surface hardness in TC21 alloy after thermal oxidation, and a 50% increase in microhardness for oxidized Titanium Grade 5 alloy [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The evidence also indicates that oxide layer thickness and phase composition are important determinants of hardness: thicker oxide layers at higher temperatures are associated with higher hardness, and TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ phases contribute to the hardness increase [N1-F1][N5-R3][N7-R1]. At the same time, the same literature notes that higher temperatures can reduce protective quality and introduce brittleness or spallation [N1-F1][N6-R1], so the relationship is not simply positive. The temperature-dependent hardness trends show that higher oxidation temperatures often improve hardness, but the literature also includes some reports of decreased mechanical properties after oxidation, which the evidence is less explicit about but suggests a nuanced dependence [N1-F1][N7-R4].

For wear resistance, oxidation generally improves performance, with the evidence showing that oxidation improves tribological properties of Titanium Grade 5 alloy, significantly increases wear resistance, and reduces wear rate in Ti6Al4V [N3-R1][N5-R5][N5-R4]. The protective oxide layer is described as reducing direct contact and abrasive wear, and as a barrier that can improve wear resistance [N4-F4][N1-F1]. However, the evidence also shows that oxide removal during sliding can lead to high friction and corrosion, which can reduce effectiveness [N4-F4]. The tribological performance under different contact conditions further shows that oxidation can be particularly beneficial in boundary lubrication, where TO-treated material showed significant improvement in wear resistance in sliding–rolling contact with a steel surface [N4-R1]. The evidence also suggests that dry sliding and fretting conditions are influenced by oxide spallation or removal, and that surface texturing or solid lubricants can help reduce friction and wear under dry conditions [N8-R2][N8-R3]. So, oxidation generally improves wear resistance, but the magnitude of improvement depends on whether the oxide remains intact and on the contact mode.

The most important oxide phases for mechanical performance are TiO₂ and Al₂O₃. TiO₂ is the dominant protective oxide formed by inward oxygen diffusion and is the main phase associated with improved hardness and wear resistance [N1-F1][N2-R5]. Al₂O₃ is important because it affects hot corrosion resistance [N1-F1], and in some contexts it can contribute to a harder oxide layer [N1-F1]. TiO₂ polymorphs, particularly rutile, are also important because their evolution with heating is described in the oxidation-induced phase study [N2-F2]. However, TiO₂ can also be brittle and spall off [N1-F1], which means that while TiO₂ is usually the most relevant protective phase, its brittleness introduces a trade-off. The literature therefore points to TiO₂ as the most important phase for protective and mechanical performance, while Al₂O₃ and other oxides are secondary contributors that can also influence hardness and corrosion resistance [N1-F1][N2-R5][N2-F2].

The trade-offs and contradictions in the literature are important. On one hand, oxidation generally improves hardness and wear resistance, with thicker oxide layers, TiO₂ formation, and Al₂O₃ presence associated with better performance [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R5][N5-R4]. On the other hand, higher temperatures can reduce protective quality, introduce brittleness, or cause oxide spallation, which can weaken the oxide layer and reduce performance [N1-F1][N6-R1]. In summary, oxidation-induced phase changes and surface morphology jointly affect hardness and wear resistance by creating a protective oxide layer composed mainly of TiO₂, which can increase hardness and improve wear resistance, while also introducing porosity, roughness, cracks, and possible spallation that can reduce performance [N1-F1][N2-R5][N2-F2][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5][N4-F4]. By contrast, oxidation improves the protective oxide layer, which can reduce abrasive wear and mitigate direct metal-to-metal contact. The TC21 study reports that the oxidized sample had the least weight loss after 10,000 m and the best wear resistance, while the nonoxidized alloy had the highest weight loss and worst wear resistance [N3-F3]. Another source explains that the protective oxide layer can be removed during sliding, which can lead to high friction and corrosion [N4-F4], suggesting that the oxide layer acts as a barrier that prevents direct interaction between the surfaces and thereby reduces wear. The evidence also notes that oxide layer formation enhances tribological performance because the oxide is protective and can improve wear resistance [N7-R1].

The literature also indicates that oxidation can alter wear resistance in different contact conditions. In boundary lubrication, the TO-treated material showed significant improvement in wear resistance in sliding–rolling contact with a steel surface [N4-R1]. In dry sliding, titanium alloys are described as having a dramatic rise in wear rate when subjected to stress [N4-F4], and one source reports that the oxidation process improved tribological properties of Titanium Grade 5 alloy [N3-R1]. For fretting wear, the evidence is more indirect but still relevant: one study involves understanding the fretting wear behavior of Ti-6Al-4V alloy under fretting conditions [N8-R2], and another reports that surface texturing and solid lubricants can substantially reduce friction and wear under dry conditions [N8-R3]. While the evidence provided here does not give a direct comparison of oxidation effects across all contact modes, it does show that oxidation tends to be beneficial in boundary lubrication and that the protective oxide layer can reduce wear in dry sliding and fretting-like conditions [N4-R1][N4-F4][N8-R2].

A key difference between conditions is that oxidation can help more in boundary lubrication and wear regimes where direct contact and friction are reduced by the oxide layer, while dry sliding and fretting may still be affected by oxide spallation, oxide removal, or direct metal-to-metal interaction [N4-F4][N4-R1][N8-R2]. The evidence also suggests that the oxide layer is not always perfectly protective; in some contexts, it can be brittle or prone to spallation, which may reduce its effectiveness [N1-F1]. Overall, oxidation generally improves wear resistance, but the extent of improvement depends on oxide layer quality, contact conditions, and whether the oxide remains intact during sliding [N3-R1][N5-R1][N5-R4][N4-R1][N4-F4].

## 4) Integrated relationship between oxidation, surface structure, phase composition, and mechanical properties

The integrated relationship is that oxidation is not a simple surface passivation effect; it changes both the physical morphology and chemical composition of the surface in ways that jointly affect hardness and wear resistance. The evidence shows that oxidation forms an oxide layer, but the quality and performance of that layer depend on the oxide phases present, the surface morphology developed, and the oxidation conditions such as temperature and time [N1-R2][N1-R4][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R5][N2-R5][N2-F2].

Oxidation-induced phase changes and surface morphology jointly affect hardness and wear resistance through a complex interplay of protective and damaging effects. On the surface structure side, oxidation can produce dense, porous, cracked, and rough oxide layers, with higher temperatures and longer times usually leading to thicker oxide layers but also more porosity and roughness [N1-R2][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R5]. The same evidence indicates that oxide layer thickness increases with both temperature and time, while porosity and roughness can also increase, especially at excessively high temperatures [N1-F1][N6-R1]. This means that the oxide layer can be both beneficial and problematic: it can protect and harden the surface, but it can also become brittle, spall off, or degrade the surface quality [N1-F1][N6-R1].

On the phase composition side, oxidation produces not just a single oxide, but a mixture of titanium oxides that evolves with heating. The evidence notes that titanium can form multiple oxides including TiO₂, TiO, Ti₃O₅, and Ti₂O₃, and that these oxides have very different properties [N2-R5]. Another source shows that TiO₂ polymorphs coexist up to 800 °C, and complete conversion to rutile occurs at higher temperatures [N2-F2]. The TC21 study also explicitly states that TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ phases formed at 800 °C contributed to the hardness increase [N1-F1]. This means that the oxide layer is not static; it changes with temperature, and the presence of TiO₂ and other oxides can influence the mechanical response. TiO₂ is described as the stable, adhesive, and protective layer formed by inward oxygen diffusion [N1-F1], but it can also be brittle and prone to spallation [N1-F1]. Al₂O₃ is noted as affecting hot corrosion resistance [N1-F1], suggesting that phase composition matters for both mechanical and environmental performance.

Taken together, these phase changes and surface morphology changes jointly affect hardness and wear resistance. Oxidation generally increases hardness, with evidence showing a threefold increase in surface hardness in TC21 alloy after thermal oxidation, and a 50% increase in microhardness for oxidized Titanium Grade 5 alloy [N1-F1][N3-F3]. The evidence also indicates that oxide layer thickness and phase composition are important determinants of hardness: thicker oxide layers at higher temperatures are associated with higher hardness, and TiO₂ and Al₂O₃ phases contribute to the hardness increase [N1-F1][N5-R3][N7-R1]. At the same time, the same literature notes that higher temperatures can reduce protective quality and introduce brittleness or spallation, which can weaken the oxide layer and reduce performance [N1-F1][N6-R1]. The temperature-dependent hardness trends show that higher oxidation temperatures often improve hardness, but the literature also includes some reports of decreased mechanical properties after oxidation, which the evidence is less explicit about but suggests a nuanced dependence [N1-F1][N7-R4].

For wear resistance, oxidation generally improves performance, with the evidence showing that oxidation improves tribological properties of Titanium Grade 5 alloy, significantly increases wear resistance, and reduces wear rate in Ti6Al4V [N3-R1][N5-R5][N5-R4]. The protective oxide layer is described as reducing direct contact and abrasive wear, and as a barrier that can improve wear resistance [N4-F4][N1-F1]. However, the evidence also shows that oxide removal during sliding can lead to high friction and corrosion, which can reduce effectiveness [N4-F4]. The tribological performance under different contact conditions further shows that oxidation can be particularly beneficial in boundary lubrication, where TO-treated material showed significant improvement in wear resistance in sliding–rolling contact with a steel surface [N4-R1]. The evidence also suggests that dry sliding and fretting conditions are influenced by oxide spallation or removal, and that surface texturing or solid lubricants can help reduce friction and wear under dry conditions [N8-R2][N8-R3]. So, oxidation generally improves wear resistance, but the magnitude of improvement depends on whether the oxide remains intact and on the contact mode.

The most important oxide phases for mechanical performance are TiO₂ and Al₂O₃. TiO₂ is the dominant protective oxide formed by inward oxygen diffusion and is the main phase associated with improved hardness and wear resistance [N1-F1][N2-R5]. Al₂O₃ is important because it affects hot corrosion resistance [N1-F1], and in some contexts it can contribute to a harder oxide layer [N1-F1]. TiO₂ polymorphs, particularly rutile, are also important because their evolution with heating is described in the oxidation-induced phase study [N2-F2]. However, TiO₂ can also be brittle and spall off [N1-F1], which means that while TiO₂ is usually the most relevant protective phase, its brittleness introduces a trade-off. The literature therefore points to TiO₂ as the most important phase for protective and mechanical performance, while Al₂O₃ and other oxides are secondary contributors that can also influence hardness and corrosion resistance [N1-F1][N2-R5][N2-F2].

---

## 5) Trade-offs and contradictions in the literature

The literature is broadly consistent with the conclusion that thermal oxidation can improve hardness and wear resistance, but it is not universally beneficial. The trade-offs are that higher temperatures often improve hardness, but can also reduce protective quality, introduce brittleness, or cause oxide spallation, which can weaken the oxide layer and reduce performance [N1-F1][N6-R1]. The evidence also shows that oxide layer integrity determines whether wear resistance improves or diminishes: a dense, intact oxide layer improves performance, while a porous, cracked, or spalled oxide layer can reduce it [N1-R2][N1-R4][N6-R2][N6-R5]. Similarly, the evidence shows that oxidation can improve wear resistance in boundary lubrication, while dry sliding and fretting may still be affected by oxide removal or direct contact [N4-R1][N4-F4][N8-R2]. 

The literature is not fully contradictory; it is more nuanced. It is broadly consistent with the conclusion that oxidation can improve mechanical performance, but only when the oxide layer remains intact and the contact conditions are favorable [N1-F1][N3-F3][N5-R5][N5-R4][N4-R1][N8-R2]. The evidence supports the idea that oxidation-induced phase changes and surface morphology jointly affect hardness and wear resistance, and that the most important oxide phases are TiO₂ and Al₂O₃, with TiO₂ being the dominant protective and mechanical contributor [N1-F1][N2-R5][N2-F2].
